python.message: Bare 'except' clause catches all exceptions including system exits.
python.description: Use 'except Exception as e:' to catch only application-level exceptions and avoid swallowing KeyboardInterrupt or SystemExit.

python.message: Use of eval() is a security risk — it executes arbitrary code.
python.description: Avoid eval(). Use ast.literal_eval() for parsing literals, or restructure logic to remove the need for dynamic evaluation.

python.message: Use of exec() is a security risk — it executes arbitrary code strings.
python.description: exec() can execute any Python code passed to it, making it dangerous with untrusted input. Refactor to avoid it.

python.message: Wildcard import ('from module import *') pollutes the namespace.
python.description: Wildcard imports make it unclear which names are in scope and can cause silent name collisions. Import only what you need.

python.message: Use 'is None' instead of '== None' for identity comparison.
python.description: Comparing to None with '==' can be overridden by __eq__. Always use 'is None' or 'is not None' for None checks.

python.message: Mutable default argument (list) detected — shared across all calls.
python.description: Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition. Use 'None' as default and create the list inside the function body.

python.message: Mutable default argument (dict) detected — shared across all calls.
python.description: Same issue as mutable list defaults. Use 'None' and initialise inside the function.
Consider resolving or tracking this comment in your issue tracker before shipping.

python.message: print() call found — remove debug output before production.
python.description: Debug print statements left in production code can leak sensitive data. Use the logging module instead.

python.message: 'pass' in block — possibly an unimplemented section.
python.description: A bare 'pass' may indicate an empty function, class, or except block that needs a real implementation.

javascript.message: Use of eval() is dangerous — executes arbitrary code and disables optimisations.
javascript.description: eval() runs a string as JavaScript. It opens XSS vectors and prevents V8/SpiderMonkey from optimising the surrounding scope.

javascript.message: document.write() is unsafe and blocks page rendering.
javascript.description: document.write() replaces the entire document when called after load. Use DOM manipulation methods like createElement/appendChild instead.

javascript.message: Direct innerHTML assignment can introduce XSS vulnerabilities.
javascript.description: If any part of the assigned string comes from user input, it becomes an XSS vector. Use textContent for text or sanitise HTML before insertion.

javascript.message: Use of 'var' — prefer 'const' or 'let' for block-scoped variables.
javascript.description: 'var' is function-scoped and hoisted, leading to subtle bugs. ES6+ 'const' and 'let' provide block scoping and clearer intent.

javascript.message: Loose equality (==) found — consider strict equality (===).
javascript.description: '==' performs type coercion (e.g. 0 == '0' is true). Use '===' to compare value and type without coercion.

javascript.message: console statement found — remove debug output before production.
javascript.description: Leaving console statements in production clutters the browser console and may expose sensitive data.

javascript.message: setTimeout with a string argument evaluates code like eval().
javascript.description: Passing a string to setTimeout is equivalent to eval(). Pass a function reference instead: setTimeout(() => { ... }, delay).
Consider resolving or tracking this comment in your issue tracker before shipping.
Consider resolving or tracking this comment in your issue tracker before shipping.

javascript.message: Use '=== null' or check with '!= null' (or '!== null') for null comparisons.
javascript.description: Loose null comparison with '==' also matches undefined. Be explicit about which you intend.

cpp.message: gets() is unsafe and removed in C11/C++14 — use fgets() instead.
cpp.description: gets() performs no bounds checking and always causes a buffer overflow vulnerability. Replace with fgets(buf, size, stdin).

cpp.message: system() executes shell commands — dangerous with any user-controlled input.
cpp.description: system() passes a string to the OS shell. If any part comes from user input this is a command injection vulnerability.

cpp.message: strcpy() performs no bounds check — use strncpy() or std::string.
cpp.description: strcpy() copies until a null terminator with no size limit, leading to buffer overflows. Use strncpy(dst, src, sizeof(dst)-1) or std::string.

cpp.message: sprintf() has no buffer size limit — use snprintf() instead.
cpp.description: sprintf() can overflow the destination buffer. Replace with snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), fmt, ...) to enforce a size limit.

cpp.message: 'goto' statement detected — consider restructuring with loops or functions.
cpp.description: goto makes control flow hard to follow and maintain. Use structured alternatives like loops, break, continue, or helper functions.

cpp.message: printf() called with a variable as the format string — format string injection risk.
cpp.description: If the first argument to printf is a user-controlled string, attackers can exploit format specifiers. Always use printf("%s", str).

cpp.message: Raw 'new' detected — ensure corresponding 'delete' exists to avoid memory leaks.
cpp.description: Each 'new' must be paired with 'delete' (or 'delete[]' for arrays). Prefer smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) in modern C++.

cpp.message: malloc() detected — prefer 'new' in C++ or use smart pointers.
cpp.description: malloc() does not call constructors and returns void*, requiring a cast. Prefer new/delete or RAII containers in C++.
Consider resolving or tracking this comment in your issue tracker before shipping.

cpp.message: 'using namespace std' in global scope can cause name collisions.
cpp.description: Pulling in all of std at global scope can silently shadow or conflict with your own names. Prefer explicit 'std::' prefix or limit the using directive to a small scope.
